system_prompt: You are annotating biomedical abstracts for a metabolic pathway-disease relation database. You follow the annotation guide exactly and never infer a claim from background knowledge that the abstract itself does not state.
guide_text:
# Task

Decide what THIS ABSTRACT claims about the relation between ONE pathway and ONE
disease. Both are already identified for you: every mention of the pathway is
wrapped in [[PATHWAY]] ... [[/PATHWAY]] and every mention of the disease in
[[DISEASE]] ... [[/DISEASE]]. The markers are not part of the text. A pathway
marker may appear inside a disease marker; that is a real nesting in the source
annotation, not an error.

Judge only this one pair. Other pathways and diseases in the abstract are left
unmarked and are not your concern.

# Labels — exactly one per pair

`upregulation`
    The abstract states the pathway's activity, expression or flux is INCREASED,
    activated or overexpressed in the disease.

    `enriched` is deliberately absent from both this list and `association`. It
    is used two ways in this literature - a pathway described as enriched in a
    condition, and a pathway merely named by an enrichment analysis - and no
    wording rule separated them reliably. Judge it by the general definitions and
    by the reference point below, and use `confidence: low` when it is unclear.
    - "Glycolytic flux was markedly higher in tumour tissue than in matched
      normal tissue." -> upregulation
    - "MTHFD2 was overexpressed in glioma tissues" -> upregulation

`downregulation`
    The abstract states it is DECREASED, impaired, suppressed, deficient or
    defective in the disease. The test is loss of function: `impaired`,
    `deficient`, `defective` and `reduced` assert that the pathway does less than
    it should, and belong here. Words that assert only that its regulation is
    disordered - `disturbed`, `perturbed`, `dysregulated` - assert no loss and
    belong to `association`. Inborn errors of metabolism belong here: a disease
    defined as a defect of a pathway states that pathway is down.
    - "Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of
      glycosphingolipid metabolism caused by the deficient activity of ..."
      -> downregulation
    - "fatty acid oxidation is reduced in SOD1 ALS fibroblasts" -> downregulation

`association`
    The abstract claims the pathway is CHANGED or INVOLVED in the disease but
    states NO direction. Typical wording: altered, dysregulated, perturbed,
    disturbed, associated with, implicated in, plays a role in, differed between
    groups, reprogrammed.
    - "The TCA cycle was significantly affected in both young and middle-aged MDD
      patients" -> association
    - "Alterations in multiple metabolic pathways, including purine, arginine and
      proline metabolism, were also associated with CAC in women with SLE."
      -> association
    An intervention claim is not `association`; see the rule below.

`no_association_stated`
    The abstract reports that it LOOKED and found NO relation. An explicit claim
    of absence is evidence, and it is not the same as silence.
    - "Higher CAP values are associated with low serum 25(OH)D concentrations but
      not with common vitamin D pathway gene variants." -> no_association_stated
    - "Markers of skeletal muscle mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation were
      also unaltered." -> no_association_stated

`none`
    The abstract makes no claim connecting this pathway to this disease. The two
    are merely co-mentioned, or the pathway is discussed in a context (a cell
    line, a different organism, a drug's metabolism, a definition sentence) that
    is not a claim about this disease.
    - An abstract about diatom metabolism that opens "BMAA is an environmental
      factor connected to neurodegenerative diseases" makes no claim about the
      diatom's urea cycle in neurodegenerative disease -> none

# Interventions

When the only claim is that acting on the pathway treats, prevents or sensitizes
the disease, read the sign from the direction of the intervention that helps:

    inhibiting / blocking / depleting the pathway helps  -> upregulation
    activating / supplementing / restoring it helps      -> downregulation

    - "Inhibiting GTP synthesis radiosensitizes GBM cells and patient-derived
      neurospheres by impairing DNA repair." -> upregulation
    - "MTX acts as an inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, leading to suppression
      of purine and pyrimidine synthesis in high metabolic and turnover cells,
      targeting cancer and dysregulated immune cells." -> upregulation

This is the one place the guide asks you to read past what is literally written:
the abstract states the effect of the intervention, not the state of the pathway
in the disease. Apply it only when the intervention and the disease are both
named, and use `confidence: medium` unless the sentence is unambiguous.

If the abstract states BOTH the pathway's state in the disease and an
intervention, label the state and quote the state sentence.

If the abstract names an intervention but not the disease it treats, that is
`none`, not a signed label.

# Reference point for `upregulation` / `downregulation`

The sign is relative to the comparison the abstract itself makes — disease versus
healthy where available, otherwise the comparison stated (resistant versus
sensitive cells, one subtype versus another, patients with a feature versus
without). If the abstract makes no comparison at all, the label is `association`
or `none`, not a guessed sign.

# `evidence`

A list of one to three sentences, each copied CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER from the
abstract, that together carry the claim. Do not paraphrase, do not merge two
sentences into one string, do not fix typography, and do not copy the
[[PATHWAY]] / [[DISEASE]] markers into a quote - they are not part of the text. A quote that is not found in
the abstract verbatim causes the row to be discarded.

Quote one sentence when one sentence states the claim. Quote more only when the
claim is genuinely split - typically when the pathway and the disease are named
in different sentences, and a third sentence is what connects them. Quote the
fewest sentences that let a reader check the label without reading the abstract.

`none` takes an empty list.

# `confidence`

`high`    the sentence states the claim plainly.
`medium`  the claim is present but requires reading across the sentence.
`low`     you are unsure between two labels.

# Output

Return ONLY a JSON object:

{"label": "...", "confidence": "...", "evidence": ["...", "..."]}

No prose before or after. No markdown fences.
note: same_sentence stratum of the 2k rebuild; every pair of every abstract that carries both entity types, no doc_level subsampling. Opus 5 was abandoned for this corpus: its safeguards refused 22.5% of a 40-pair probe, deterministically.
